text: Kanzan Shimomura was a pseudonym. His real name was Shimomura Seizaburō. He was born in Wakayama into a family of hereditary Noh actors and moved to Tokyo at eight. There he studied under Kanō Hōgai, and after Hōgai's death under Hashimoto Gahō. He graduated first in his class at the Tōkyō Bijutsu Gakkō and became a teacher there in 1894. When Okakura Tenshin left government service to found the Japan Fine Arts Academy, Kanzan joined him together with Yokoyama Taikan and Hishida Shunsō. He later spent two years studying in England, and in 1914 he helped re-establish the Academy.

Miloš Jiránek was a Czech Neo-Impressionist painter who also worked as an art critic and writer. As a schoolboy in Prague he lived with the poet Jaroslav Vrchlický, who had a huge library, and he read many books in the original languages. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts under Maximilian Pirner and then Vojtěch Hynais. In 1897 he joined the Mánes Union of Fine Arts. In 1900 he went to the Exposition Universelle in Paris, where he met Auguste Rodin. A few years later he played a major role in introducing the works of Rodin and Edvard Munch.

Piercy Roberts was an English publisher, printmaker and caricaturist. Most of his prints are caricatures, some from his own designs and some after others such as George Moutard Woodward. He worked with Thomas Rowlandson on a pair of portraits of Josephine Beauharnais and Napoleon. In 1801 he put himself in a print called Caricature Shop, standing in the doorway of his own print shop in Holborn while a crowd of onlookers studies his window. It is one of the best depictions of a print shop. He eventually sold up to Thomas Tegg in 1806.

Tosa Mitsunori was a painter of the Tosa school, the son of Tosa Mitsuyoshi and the father of Tosa Mitsuoki. He moved to Sakai in his youth. He sometimes presented painted fans to the Sentō Imperial Palace, but he never received a position at the court. At about 52 he went back to Kyoto with his eldest son Mitsuoki. He made many small works with gold backgrounds that kept up the Tosa tradition. One of the few surviving works is a scroll, the Legend of the Taima mandala, painted in a quite conservative style.

William Derby was born in Birmingham, where Joseph Barber taught him drawing. He moved to London in 1808. His first job there was making reduced drawings for the plates of the Stafford Gallery, a set of engravings of the paintings in the Marquess of Stafford's collection. After that he worked as a portrait and miniature painter and sometimes made watercolour copies of notable pictures. In 1825 he took over from William Hilton the drawings for Lodge's Portraits of Illustrious Personages of Great Britain. The job meant copying paintings in collections across the country, and he made many useful introductions along the way.

Lucas de Heere was born in Ghent, the second son of a sculptor and a miniaturist. His father trained him. He had a brother and four sisters. He worked as a painter, print artist, poet and playwright, and his costume books and portraits are useful for knowing what people wore in the 16th century. We know about his life mostly from Het Schilder-Boeck, which was written by his pupil Karel van Mander.

Jacob van Swanenburg was a teacher of the young Rembrandt. He was born in Leiden, where his father Isaac was the leading history painter and served several times as mayor. Isaac had trained under Frans Floris in Antwerp. Jacob spent a substantial part of his early career in Italy before returning home, and he painted city views, history paintings, religious scenes and portraits. He dealt in art too. His younger brothers Claes and Willem became a painter and a printmaker.

Anthony Velonis was a New York painter and designer who helped bring silkscreen printing to the public. While working for the federal Works Progress Administration during the Great Depression, he moved silkscreen into the mainstream as a fine art form, which came to be called the serigraph. At his own request he was not publicly credited for coining that term. He mastered how to print on glass, plastics and metal. Later in the century, artists such as Robert Rauschenberg and Andy Warhol took up the technique. He married Elizabeth Amidon, and they had four children.

Girolamo dai Libri learned to illuminate manuscripts from his father Francesco. He most likely also attended the workshop of Domenico Morone, where he made friends with Morone's son Francesco. They later collaborated on several commissions. As a young man he made miniatures, especially for the convent of Santa Maria in Organo in Verona. According to Vasari, he astonished his contemporaries when he painted the altarpiece Deposition from the Cross for the same church at about 25. He worked in an early Renaissance style.

Lluís Borrassà learned painting from his father, Honorat. He is first documented in 1380 as a member of the court of John I of Aragon. In 1390 he set up a workshop in Barcelona that stayed the city's largest until 1420. He is widely considered to have introduced the International Gothic style to Catalonia. His workshop produced many narrative altarpieces. One for the convent church of St. Damien was often praised, but it has since disappeared. Bernat Martorell was influenced by him.

Matteo Giovannetti was born in Viterbo and worked mostly in Avignon as a member of the papal court. Pope Clement VI summoned him there to decorate the Palais des Papes. He led teams of painters from right across Europe. In 1344 he began painting the Saint-Martial chapel, a small chapel attached to the great dining hall, and he finished it the next year. He also decorated the Saint-Michel oratory. People often place him in the school of Simone Martini because of similar styles, but there is no evidence that the two ever met.

Adolf Kašpar was the son of a general wares dealer in Bludov. He studied at the Prague Academy under Maxmilián Pirner. His mentor was Hanus Schwaiger, a famous painter and children's book illustrator, who recommended him to the academy and influenced his life and art. Kašpar became famous for illustrating The Grandmother, a book by Božena Němcová. He also illustrated works by Alois Jirásek, Jan Neruda, Karel Václav Rais and František Ladislav Čelakovský. To get his pieces right, he collected information from Czech literature.

Ferdinand Bac was born Ferdinand-Sigismond Bach in Stuttgart, and his father was an illegitimate nephew of the Emperor Napoleon. As a young man he mixed in the fashionable world of Paris and became known for caricatures in popular journals. He travelled widely too. In his fifties he started a new career as a landscape gardener. His gardens at Les Colombières in Menton are now listed as a Monument Historique. He wrote a great deal about social, historical and political subjects, but most of it has been forgotten.

Isabella Piccini was born Elisabetta in Venice, where her father Giacomo was an etcher and engraver, and he trained her in engraving and illustration in the style of masters such as Rubens and Titian. In 1666 she became a Franciscan nun at the Convent of Santa Croce. She took the name Sister Isabella. Prominent Italians commissioned portraits and religious works from her. Giovanni Antonio Remondini sold her prints across Europe. She split all her income between her convent and her family.

Pantaleon Szyndler took his first art lessons at the School of Fine Arts in Warsaw with Rafał Hadziewicz, and a scholarship from the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts let him study abroad. He spent three years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. Then he went to the Accademia di San Luca in Rome and finished in Paris. He painted in the Academic style. Most of his pictures are nudes, religious works and Orientalist scenes. Some canvases were inspired by Polish Romantic poetry, and he was a close friend of Cyprian Norwid.

Walter Crane argued for anti-authoritarian democratic socialism among British socialists and in the labour movement. He produced a large body of work. Some of it was apolitical, mostly illustrations for children's books and general-interest literature of the Victorian era, and some carried explicit political messages. He is considered one of the most influential and prolific children's book designers of his generation. He lived from 1845 to 1915.

Martin Schongauer was the most important printmaker north of the Alps before Dürer, who collected his work. He came from Colmar and was known to his contemporaries as Martin Schön, or pretty Martin. He seems to have had the family background and training in goldsmithing that was usual for early engravers. Most of his surviving production is 116 engravings, all with his monogram but none dated. They were well known in Germany and Italy. He died in 1491.

George Morland's publishers made much more money from his prints than he did, since a lot of his work was meant for reproduction. His early work followed Francis Wheatley, but after the 1790s he found his own style. His best compositions are rustic scenes of farms and hunting, smugglers and gypsies, and rich landscapes influenced by Dutch Golden Age painting. He drank heavily and lived a rackety life. He was enormously prolific, though quality suffered. He died at 41.

George Stubbs taught himself to paint, independently of the great artists of the 18th century like Reynolds and Gainsborough. He is best known for horses, but his output includes history paintings too. His greatest skill was painting animals, maybe because of his love and study of anatomy. His series on a lion attacking a horse are early and significant examples of Romanticism. He enjoyed royal patronage. Whistlejacket hangs in the National Gallery in London.

Foreign visitors on the Grand Tour poured into Rome, and Pompeo Batoni specialised in portraits of them. His sitters were mostly British and Anglo-Irish gentlemen, often shown with famous Italian landscapes behind. These portraits ended up in British private collections and spread the genre's popularity in Britain. He also painted numerous allegorical and mythological pictures, with solid technical knowledge. He lived from 1708 to 1787.

Peasants, soldiers and other lower-class people drinking, smoking, playing cards or fighting in taverns are the subjects that made Adriaen Brouwer an innovator of genre painting. He also helped develop the tronie, a head or facial study that explores varieties of expression. In his last year he painted a few landscapes of tragic intensity. He worked in Flanders and the Dutch Republic. He had an important influence on the next generation of Flemish and Dutch genre painters. He died in 1638.

Robert Duncanson, a free Black man in antebellum America, spent most of his career in Cincinnati and helped develop the Ohio River Valley landscape tradition. Thomas Cole and other American landscape artists inspired him, and he counts as a second-generation Hudson River School painter. He worked with the abolitionist community in America and England to support and promote his work. He is considered the first African-American artist to be known internationally. He died in 1872.

Franz Anton Maulbertsch studied at the Academy of Vienna. Through Paul Troger he came to know the Venetian painters Piazzetta and Pittoni. He studied Sebastiano Ricci's frescoes in the Schönbrunn Palace and spent time with Giambattista Tiepolo, who was in Würzburg from 1750. He was an appreciated frescoer, and most commissions were for churches. He painted in Rococo style in the German and Hungarian regions. He lived from 1724 to 1796.

Francesco Zuccarelli is considered the most important landscape painter to emerge from Venice in the mid-eighteenth century. His Arcadian views became popular across Europe, and especially in England, where he lived for two long periods. His patrons included the nobility. He often worked with other artists such as Antonio Visentini and Bernardo Bellotto. In 1768 he became a founding member of the Royal Academy. He died in 1788.

Bernhard Strigel came from Memmingen and probably studied with Zeitblom at Ulm. He was the most important member of a family of artists based in Memmingen. Emperor Maximilian I held him in high favor, and Strigel repeatedly travelled for him to Augsburg, Innsbruck and Vienna. His religious paintings include four altar wings in the Berlin Gallery and ten pictures of the Genealogy of Christ in Nuremberg. They are of less artistic value than his portraits. He died in 1528.

For centuries nobody could attribute Giovanni Agostino da Lodi's works with confidence, until Bernard Berenson defined his style and career. One of his first identified pieces is the Boatmen Altarpiece in the church of San Pietro Martire at Murano. His only signed work is a pair of saints in the Brera, which shows Lombard influences such as Bramantino's. Leonardo's style influenced him later. He was active from about 1495 to 1525.

Rik Wouters made some 200 works in his 34 years. Illness killed him partway through the First World War, in Amsterdam. He was a sculptor, painter, draughtsman and etcher in a typically Fauvist style, and his art resembled that of Matisse, Cézanne and Derain. One writer says his work reflects warmth and tenderness. His paintings use many colours and brush strokes and often leave canvas unpainted.

Ilya Repin grew up in Chuguev, then part of Russia. He became one of the most famous artists in Russia in the 19th century. His major works include Barge Haulers on the Volga, Religious Procession in Kursk Province, Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan, and Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks. He also painted revealing portraits of Glinka, Mussorgsky, Pavel Tretyakov and Leo Tolstoy, with whom he had a long friendship. He died in 1930.

Louis Marcoussis studied law in Warsaw before attending the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts. He then moved to Paris to study under Jules Lefebvre at the Académie Julian. His first major exhibition was at the Salon d'Automne in 1905. In the cafes of Montmartre and Montparnasse he got to know artists and writers. Guillaume Apollinaire, who had Polish roots too, suggested his French name. He died in 1941.

James Longacre ran away to Philadelphia at twelve and became an apprentice in a bookstore. His artistic talent showed, and he was released to apprentice at an engraving firm. He struck out on his own in 1819, providing illustrations for popular biographies. From 1844 until his death he was the fourth chief engraver of the United States Mint. Best known for the Indian Head cent of 1859. He also designed the Shield nickel.

Jan van Kessel the Elder came from the Brueghel family, and many of his subjects took inspiration from his grandfather Jan Brueghel the Elder. He worked in Antwerp in the mid-17th century. He painted insects, flowers, marines, river landscapes, paradise landscapes and allegories, and also animals and genre scenes. His contemporaries prized his works highly. Daniel Seghers and Frans Snyders also inspired him. He died in 1679.
